sections.Run Context: Authoritative inputs: TARGET_AGENT_PATH=examples/call-for-papers-mcp; GUIDANCE_FILE=smith/guidance.txt; SYSTEM_VAR_FILE=smith/system_vars.json; TOOL_DEFINITIONS_FILE=smith/tool_definitions.json (manually-maintained; live MCP refresh failed due to a missing Python dependency in the example server, treated as authoritative per workflow contract). Source files inspected: agent.py (FastAPI HTTP layer + LangGraph ReAct agent + MCP client wiring), server.py (FastMCP tool registration, stdio transport), app.py (WikiCFPScraper implementation + getEvents business logic). requirements.txt and smith/mcp_tool_summary.md reviewed for corroborating context. No test, cache, or generated-analysis files were needed to resolve tool behavior; zero unresolved paths remain.
sections.Trust Boundaries: (1) HTTP client -> agent.py /chat and /extract_tool_call endpoints: caller-supplied `question` and `user_profile` (arbitrary dict) cross into the process untrusted; `user_profile` is interpolated verbatim into the LLM system prompt by build_system_prompt with no schema validation, so any subject/system-var claims are unauthenticated and self-asserted by the caller. (2) LLM agent -> MCP server (server.py) over stdio: the LLM decides tool name and arguments (keywords, topic, limit); this is the natural pre-execution enforcement boundary since it is structured and fully visible before app.py executes. (3) MCP tool handler (server.py) -> app.py getEvents: server.py drops the `topic` argument entirely when calling getEvents(keywords, limit) — topic never crosses this boundary despite being declared/required in the tool schema. (4) app.py -> external WikiCFP service over plain HTTP: unauthenticated, unverified scraped HTML re-enters the trust boundary as tool output returned to the LLM/user.
sections.Data Flow: Request: HTTP caller -> agent.py (/chat: question + optional user_profile folded into system prompt text; /extract_tool_call: single non-executing LLM call that only extracts intended tool_name/arguments, does not invoke WikiCFP) -> LangGraph react agent selects `get_events` tool with args {keywords, topic, limit} -> MCP client (stdio) -> server.py get_events(keywords, topic, limit) -> calls app.getEvents(keywords, limit) [topic silently dropped] -> WikiCFPScraper.search_conferences issues GET to http://www.wikicfp.com/cfp/servlet/tool.search?q=<keywords>&year=t. Response: raw HTML -> BeautifulSoup parse -> list of conference dicts -> sliced to `limit` -> {status, count, events} returned up through server.py -> MCP client -> LangGraph agent -> final LLM message -> ChatResponse to HTTP caller.

Enforcement Points.Available (OPA-interceptable): keywords, topic, limit are all structured, fully visible tool arguments at this boundary before any external call is made — an OPA policy call inserted here could evaluate topic membership, limit bounds/role caps, and role/guest gating using input.args.* and input.extensions.subject.* (if subject fields were actually threaded through as structured data instead of free text)
Enforcement Points.Blind spots: topic is dropped before reaching app.py, so even if it were policy-checked at the MCP boundary, nothing downstream re-derives or re-validates it; queries_this_session has no server-side counter, so per-session query-count limits cannot be enforced without the caller supplying a running count as a genuine structured system variable

Enforcement Points.Blind spots: Currently user_profile is free-form and unauthenticated; the LLM, not code, decides whether to honor any embedded constraint, so prompt-text-only propagation is a true blind spot until subject fields are carried as structured, verifiable data

handoff.Summary: Sources: agent.py, server.py, app.py (3 implementation files, 0 unresolved paths). Tools: 1 declared (get_events) — implementation matches tool_definitions.json in name and required/optional signature (keywords required, topic required, limit optional default 10); every declared argument (keywords, topic, limit) has an implementation-derived disposition. Layers: 4 (agent/client, MCP, tool implementation, external service) — no runtime context/enforcement layer exists in code today. Runtime subject fields: 5 declared in system_vars.json (user_role, dissertation_area, research_area, queries_this_session, user_name); none are read by any code path or exposed as OPA-visible input.extensions.subject.* fields — all are effectively undeclared-at-runtime despite being declared in the system-vars file. Undeclared fields relative to the governed schema: 3 guidance dependencies (dissertation_area, queries_this_session, user_role) have no verified runtime path into the tool schema or subject context. Key gap: the `topic` argument is required by the tool schema and used for policy-level scoping intent, but server.py silently drops it before calling app.getEvents, so it reaches the MCP boundary but never the implementation — classify as Ignored, not proof of a schema mismatch (tool_definitions.json and server.py agree on the declared signature). No enforcement exists anywhere in the current implementation; the only viable pre-execution enforcement point is the MCP tool boundary in server.py, which has full visibility into keywords/topic/limit but no verified way today to obtain user_role, dissertation_area, or queries_this_session as trustworthy structured subject data.
